title: Stainless steel doesn’t rust because it corrodes a tiny bit first
body: Stainless steel is an iron alloy with at least 10.5% chromium. The chromium reacts with oxygen in the air to form a microscopically thin, invisible film of chromium oxide on the surface. This **passive film** blocks oxygen from reaching the iron beneath, so the steel can’t rust. Best of all, it repairs itself: scratch it and, with oxygen present, fresh chromium at the surface oxidises and seals the gap. Harry Brearley of Sheffield hit on the alloy in 1913 while looking for a corrosion-resistant steel for gun barrels.

slides.heading: A film that heals
slides.text: Plain steel rusts because iron oxide is loose and lets oxygen and water keep reaching the metal. Chromium oxide is different: it forms a tight, invisible skin that stops oxygen getting through, and it re-forms wherever it is scratched or disturbed, as long as some oxygen is around.

slides.heading: How stainless steel heals a scratch

steps.label: Chromium at the surface meets oxygen
A thin, invisible chromium oxide film forms
A scratch exposes fresh metal underneath
Fresh chromium oxidises and seals the gap

slides.question: Out of 20 parts of steel by weight, how many must be chromium for it to count as stainless?
slides.explanation: At least 10.5% chromium by weight, so about 2 parts in 20. Raising it above 11% boosts the protection further, and the most common grade, type 304 or ‘18/8’, has about 18%.

slides.label: the minimum chromium content for a steel to count as stainless
slides.text: Raising the chromium above 11% boosts the resistance further.

slides.question: What happens when stainless steel gets scratched?
options: It starts to rust at once
slides.explanation: Fresh chromium at the exposed surface reacts with oxygen and rebuilds the passive film, so the scratch seals itself.
